content: 1. Kanashiro HM et al. conducted a cluster-randomized trial that evaluated the impact of complementary and responsive feeding education provided to caregivers. The study demonstrated significant improvements in dietary intake, growth, and developmental outcomes among toddlers in rural India. (Maternal and Child Nutrition, 2013; 9(1): 99-117). 2. Wagner M, Spiker D, and Linn MI assessed the effectiveness of the Parents as Teachers program, specifically targeting low-income parents and their children. Their findings highlighted the program's positive impact on early childhood development. (Topics in Early Childhood Special Education, 2002; 22(2): 67-81). 3. Walkup JT, Barlow A, Mullany BC, Pan W, Goklish N, and Hasting R et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate an in-home intervention delivered by paraprofessionals. This intervention targeted young American Indian mothers living on reservations and showed promising results in improving maternal and child outcomes. (Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 2009; 48(6): 591-601). 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) published a comprehensive handbook in 2014 to guide the development of evidence-based health guidelines. This resource serves as a foundation for improving health outcomes globally. 5. WHO, UNICEF, and the World Bank Group introduced a framework in 2018 titled Nurturing Care for Early Childhood Development. This framework emphasizes the importance of helping children survive and thrive to unlock their full health and human potential. 6. Yousafzai AK and Aboud F reviewed the implementation processes of integrated nutrition and psychosocial stimulation interventions. Their analysis provided insights into effective strategies for improving child development outcomes. (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 2014; 1308(1): 33-45). 7. Yousafzai AK, Aboud FE, Nores M, and Britto PR edited a special issue in 2018 focusing on implementation research and practices for early childhood development. (Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1419). 8. Yousafzai AK, Rasheed MA, Rizvi A, Armstrong R, and Bhutta ZA conducted a cluster-randomized factorial effectiveness trial within Pakistan's Lady Health Worker program. Their study demonstrated the positive effects of integrated responsive stimulation and nutrition interventions on child development, growth, and health outcomes. (The Lancet, 2014; 384(9950): 1282-93). 9. Yousafzai AK, Rasheed MA, Rizvi A, Armstrong R, and Bhutta ZA also conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate parenting skills and emotional availability. The study highlighted the benefits of targeted interventions in improving parent-child interactions. (Pediatrics, 2015; 135(5): e1247-57). 10. WHO guidelines and tools are instrumental in improving early childhood development (ECD). These resources address various aspects of child health, including neonatal care, nutrition, environmental health, prevention and treatment of childhood illnesses, caregiver mental health, and support for children with developmental difficulties or disabilities. 11. Optimal infant and young child feeding practices, including exclusive and continued breastfeeding, are critical for enhancing ECD. WHO provides training courses for health workers to support mothers in breastfeeding effectively. 12. WHO's integrated infant feeding counseling course equips health workers with the skills to counsel on breastfeeding, HIV and infant feeding, and complementary feeding. This five-day training is designed for primary healthcare providers and lay counselors. 13. WHO offers a combined course on growth assessment and infant feeding counseling. This course trains health workers to measure, interpret, and address growth and feeding issues, promoting appropriate practices and managing malnutrition. 14. WHO's guideline on breastfeeding counseling provides evidence-based recommendations to improve breastfeeding practices among pregnant women and mothers. It includes guidance on the frequency, timing, and mode of counseling. 15. The NetCode toolkit by WHO supports ongoing monitoring and assessment of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes. It provides protocols and tools to strengthen legislative and regulatory frameworks. 16. WHO's guideline on feeding low-birth-weight infants in lowand middle-income countries offers specific recommendations on feeding practices to improve survival and care for this high-risk population. 17. WHO's guideline on managing severe acute malnutrition in children provides evidence-based recommendations for care, including play and stimulation activities, even in the context of HIV. 18. WHO updated the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding to protect, promote, and support optimal breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities. This initiative aligns with global health goals and sustainable development targets. 19. WHO's Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) ensures timely and appropriate care for mothers and newborns, promoting optimal feeding practices and supporting breastfeeding. 20. Responsive caregiving and early learning opportunities are essential components of nurturing care. WHO materials guide health workers in helping families build stronger relationships and address caregiving challenges. 21. WHO's Care for Child Development materials recommend play and communication activities to stimulate children's learning and teach adults to respond sensitively to children's needs. 22. WHO's resources on child health, growth, and development guide health workers in counseling caregivers on feeding, responsive caregiving, early learning, illness prevention, and timely care-seeking. 23. WHO's discussion paper on early childhood development and disability highlights strategies to improve developmental outcomes and rights for children with disabilities through multisectoral approaches. 24. WHO's antenatal care recommendations emphasize nutrition, partner violence assessment, substance abuse prevention, and community-based interventions to optimize pregnancy outcomes and ECD. 25. WHO's guideline on having a companion during labor and childbirth highlights this as a low-cost, effective intervention to improve maternity care quality. 26. WHO's guideline on preventing and treating maternal peripartum infections consolidates evidence-based recommendations to reduce maternal and newborn complications. 27. WHO's guideline on improving preterm birth outcomes focuses on interventions during pregnancy, labor, and the newborn period to enhance survival and health outcomes. 28. WHO's postnatal care guideline addresses timing, frequency, and content of care for mothers and newborns in resource-limited settings, ensuring early detection of complications. 29. WHO's framework for improving maternal and newborn care quality outlines eight domains of care to be assessed and monitored within health systems. 30. WHO's Network for Improving Quality of Care provides resources, country examples, and peer exchanges to address challenges in maternal, newborn, and child health. 31. WHO's INSPIRE framework outlines seven evidence-based strategies to prevent violence against children, including laws, norms, safe environments, caregiver support, economic strengthening, response services, and education. 32. WHO's publication on evaluating parenting programs offers guidance on assessing interventions aimed at preventing violence against children. 33. WHO's Parenting for Lifelong Health program provides manuals and handbooks for facilitators and parents, focusing on parenting strategies for babies, toddlers, and young children.
